objective: By the end of this lesson you can define a runway incursion, explain the taxi clearance, recording, briefing, marking, sign, lighting and nontowered airport procedures that prevent one, manage the risks of bias, distraction, night, low visibility, landing rollout and parallel runways, and teach all of it to a student from the first lesson to the flight review.
why: Runway incursions have led to serious accidents with large loss of life, and surface movement accidents are one of the biggest safety concerns in aviation [[7:2|AC 91-73B 5]]. FAA data in the PHAK says about 65 percent of runway incursions are caused by pilots, and almost half of those by general aviation pilots [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]]. The AFH names the flight instructor as the key to teaching safe taxi practices early and throughout a pilot's career [[24:34|AFH 1-13]].

warmup: Think first: your student has flown out of the same airport for 20 hours and always gets the same taxi route. Today ground control gives a different route with a hold short of a runway the student has never crossed. The student reads back the usual route, and ground does not catch it. Where in your training did this error begin, and what habit would have stopped it before the airplane moved?

key_terms.def: Any occurrence at an aerodrome involving the incorrect presence of an aircraft, vehicle or person on the protected area of a surface designated for landing and takeoff (FAA Order 7050.1 wording) [[7:1|AC 91-73B 1]].
An action of a pilot that violates any Federal Aviation Regulation, such as crossing a hold marking or taking off without clearance [[1:365|PHAK 14-31]] [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].
A location on an airport movement area with a history of potential risk of collision or runway incursion, where pilots and drivers need heightened attention [[34:358|AIM P/C Glossary H-3]].
Precise taxi instructions given to a pilot unfamiliar with the airport, or issued in stages as the aircraft moves along the route [[34:396|AIM P/C Glossary P-5]].
Four yellow lines, two solid and two dashed, across the taxiway; the solid lines are on the side where the aircraft must hold [[33:151|AIM 2-3-5a]].
Yellow dashes on both sides of the taxiway centerline, up to 150 feet before a runway holding position marking, warning of an upcoming runway [[1:346|PHAK 14-12]].

A row of red, steady-burning in-pavement lights across the taxiway at the runway holding position, used in low visibility (below 1,200 ft RVR) to confirm a clearance to enter or cross [[33:133|AIM 2-1-10e]] [[33:134|AIM 2-1-10e]].
Automated red Runway Entrance Lights and Takeoff Hold Lights that show a runway is unsafe to enter, cross or take off on; they never convey an ATC clearance [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6a]].

Common Traffic Advisory Frequency, designated for airport advisory practices at an airport without an operating control tower; it may be a UNICOM, MULTICOM, FSS or tower frequency [[33:206|AIM 4-1-9b]].

An erroneous assessment that persists even though evidence shows it is wrong; on the ground it shows up as hearing the expected taxi route instead of the one given [[30:45|RMH 6-2]] [[30:46|RMH 6-3]].
Suppressing information that conflicts with what you expect instead of treating it as a warning; related to, but not the same as, expectation bias [[30:45|RMH 6-2]].
An ATC instruction to enter the runway and hold in position for takeoff. It is not a takeoff clearance [[1:368|PHAK 14-34]].

chunks.title: K1: What a runway incursion is, and who causes them

body.p: Teach the current definition first. AC 91-73B quotes FAA Order 7050.1: a runway incursion is any occurrence at an aerodrome involving the incorrect presence of an aircraft, vehicle or person on the protected area of a surface designated for the landing and takeoff of aircraft [[7:1|AC 91-73B 1]]. The key words for a student are 'incorrect presence' and 'protected area'. No near miss is needed; being where you were not cleared to be is enough.

The PHAK and AFH still print an older wording that requires a collision hazard or a loss of separation [[1:365|PHAK 14-31]] [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]. A student who learns only that version may think 'nothing happened, so it was not an incursion'. Correct that early.

head: Kind of event
Examples the PHAK gives
rows: Pilot deviation (PD)
Crossing a runway hold marking without ATC clearance, taking off without clearance, landing without clearance [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].
Operational incident (OI)
ATC clears an aircraft onto a runway while another is landing on it, or issues a takeoff clearance while the runway is occupied [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].
Vehicle or pedestrian deviation (V/PD)
A vehicle or person enters or moves on the runway movement area without ATC authorization [[1:365|PHAK 14-31]].

bullets: About 65 percent of runway incursions are caused by pilots; almost half of those are general aviation pilots [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].
Investigations found three main contributing areas: failure to comply with ATC instructions, lack of airport familiarity, and nonconformance with standard operating procedures [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].
The AFH groups the causes as communications, airport knowledge, and flight deck procedures for maintaining orientation [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].
Roughly three runway incursions happen each day at towered airports in the United States [[1:365|PHAK 14-31]].

callout.text: Teach it: the AFH says the flight instructor is the key to the formal teaching of safe taxi practices and should instill awareness of incursions from the start [[24:34|AFH 1-13]]. Runway incursion avoidance is also on the AIH list of common special emphasis items, and the AIH says instructors must cover every item in the ACS [[25:164|AIH 8-6]]. Make it part of every lesson, not one ground session.

check.q: Your student stops two feet past a runway hold line, sees nothing on final and says 'no harm done'. Was that a runway incursion under the AC 91-73B definition?
check.a: It can be. The definition is the incorrect presence of an aircraft on the protected area of a runway; no collision hazard is required [[7:1|AC 91-73B 1]]. Crossing a hold marking without clearance is also a pilot deviation [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].

body.p: At an airport with an operating control tower, no one may operate an aircraft on a runway or taxiway, or take off or land, without an appropriate ATC clearance [[60:454|14 CFR 91.129(i)]]. Once a clearance is obtained the pilot may not deviate from it except as the rule allows, and a pilot who is uncertain must immediately ask for clarification [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]].

head: What ATC says
What it means
rows: Runway, then route, then any hold short or crossing
When assigning a takeoff runway, ATC states the runway, gives the route, and states any hold short or crossing instructions for runways on the way [[33:260|AIM 4-3-18a]].
'Runway 27, taxi via Alpha'
Does not authorize entering or crossing the assigned departure runway at any point. ATC does not use the word 'cleared' for taxi [[33:260|AIM 4-3-18a]].
'Cross Runway 31'

ATC issues an explicit clearance for every runway crossing [[33:260|AIM 4-3-18a]], normally one runway at a time, and you must have crossed the previous runway before the next crossing is issued. This applies to active, inactive and closed runways [[1:368|PHAK 14-34]].
'Hold short of Runway 31'
Stop so no part of the aircraft extends beyond the runway holding position marking [[33:151|AIM 2-3-5a]]. ATC must get a readback of every hold short instruction [[33:260|AIM 4-3-18a]].
Taxi to parking after landing
Ground's clearance to parking does not authorize entering or crossing any runway [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]].
A standard taxi route (STR)
Does not constitute or imply a clearance to cross a runway; if you are unsure, ask or decline it [[33:263|AIM 4-3-20]].

bullets: Initial call to ground or tower: who you are, where you are on the airport, what you want, and what you know, for example 'Cessna N1234, at SeaBreeze FBO, VFR to taxi, with information Alpha' [[7:8|AC 91-73B 7f(2)]].
Always read back the runway assignment, any clearance to enter a specific runway, and any instruction to hold short of a runway or line up and wait [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18a9]].
Include the complete call sign and runway designator. Avoid 'Roger' or 'Wilco' for runway entry, hold short or LUAW [[7:8|AC 91-73B 7f(4)]].
Unfamiliar or confused: request progressive taxi, which gives step-by-step routing [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18b]].
If you cannot safely comply with any ATC instruction, say 'UNABLE'. The final decision to act rests with you [[1:367|PHAK 14-33]].

callout.text: Teach it: use the principle of primacy. Get the readback right the first time, because what is learned first is what the student falls back on [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Have the student make every call from lesson one, with you listening, rather than doing the radios yourself until 'later'.

check.q: Ground says: 'N52K, Runway 18, taxi via Bravo.' Bravo crosses Runway 9. May your student cross Runway 9?
check.a: No. ATC issues an explicit clearance for every runway crossing; stop at the Runway 9 hold line and wait for 'cross Runway 9' [[33:260|AIM 4-3-18a]] [[1:368|PHAK 14-34]].

chunks.title: K3: Record the instructions and review the route on the diagram

body.p: Complex taxi clearances can include many turns and intermediate hold short lines. Written instructions give the pilot a reference for the readback and a way to confirm the route and restrictions while moving, which guards against forgetting or misunderstanding part of the clearance [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7e]]. The PHAK adds that writing down all taxi instructions as soon as they are received reduces incursion risk [[1:367|PHAK 14-33]].

head: Step
Example from AC 91-73B
rows: Clearance received
'N123 taxi 9R via Bravo, Echo, Juliet, hold short 4L at Echo' [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7e(2)]]
Written in shorthand
9R B E J 4L E, with the clearance limit '4L at Echo' circled [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7e(2)]]
Symbols
Hold short = /, cross = X [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7e(2)]]
How much to write
Near or familiar route: the basic elements. Complex route or unfamiliar airport: a detailed transcription [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7e(1)]]

body.p: Reviewing the diagram is the other half of K3. Before taxi, review the current airport diagram, the hot spots and any published standard taxi route text to get the 'big picture' of where an incursion could happen [[7:3|AC 91-73B 7b(1)(d)]]. Trace or highlight the taxi route to the departure runway before leaving the ramp [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]]. While taxiing, follow your progress on the diagram and check the route against the heading indicator or compass, especially at hot spots and complex intersections [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7d(1)]].

callout.text: AC 91-73B highly recommends that CFIs teach students the meaning and use of airport diagrams, and that CFIs require students to have and use current diagrams for departure, arrival and alternate airports [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2) NOTE]].
Write it, read it, trace it, track it: write the clearance, read back from the paper, trace the route on the diagram, then track your progress against the diagram and the heading indicator.

check.q: How would a student write 'Runway 9R via Bravo, Echo, Juliet, hold short 4L at Echo' the AC 91-73B way?
check.a: 9R B E J 4L E, with '4L at Echo' circled as the clearance limit; '/' means hold short and 'X' means cross [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7e(2)]].

chunks.title: K4: Markings, signs and lights, and why hold lines matter most

body.p: The PHAK calls the hold sign and hold marking the most important sign and marking on the airport [[1:367|PHAK 14-33]]. Not complying with a runway holding position sign or marking may lead the FAA to file a pilot deviation against you [[1:340|PHAK 14-6]] [[1:342|PHAK 14-8]]. Runway holding position markings also generally mark the boundary of the runway safety area [[33:151|AIM 2-3-5a]].

head: Item
What it looks like
What the pilot does
rows: Runway holding position marking
Four yellow lines, two solid and two dashed; solid lines on the holding side [[33:151|AIM 2-3-5a]]
At a towered airport, do not cross without ATC clearance; at a nontowered airport, ensure separation first [[33:151|AIM 2-3-5a]].
Runway holding position sign
White inscription on a red background [[33:151|AIM 2-3-5a]]
Never let any part of the aircraft pass it without clearance from ATC [[1:342|PHAK 14-8]].
Surface painted holding position sign
Red background, white inscription, left of the taxiway centerline on the holding side [[33:152|AIM 2-3-5d]]
Supplements the vertical sign; same meaning.
Enhanced taxiway centerline
Yellow dashes on both sides of the centerline, up to 150 feet before the hold marking [[1:346|PHAK 14-12]]
Runway ahead: slow down, confirm the clearance.
ILS critical area holding position
Yellow 'ladder' across the taxiway with a red sign [[33:151|AIM 2-3-5b]]
Hold only when ATC says 'hold short of the ILS critical area'; otherwise continue [[1:346|PHAK 14-12]].
Runway guard lights
Pair of elevated flashing yellow lights or a row of in-pavement yellow lights at the hold marking [[33:133|AIM 2-1-10d]]
Taxiway/runway intersection ahead.
Stop bar
Row of red steady lights across the taxiway at the hold position, used below 1,200 ft RVR [[33:133|AIM 2-1-10e]]
Never cross a lit red stop bar, even with a clearance [[33:134|AIM 2-1-10e CAUTION]].
Runway Entrance Lights (REL)
Red in-pavement lights along the taxiway centerline toward the runway [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6b]]
Stop at the hold line or stay stopped; contact ATC if the clearance conflicts [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6b]].
Takeoff Hold Lights (THL)
Double row of red lights along the runway centerline ahead of the LUAW point [[33:128|AIM 2-1-6c]]
Safely stop or stay stopped; lights going dark is not a takeoff clearance [[33:128|AIM 2-1-6c]].

bullets: Runways have white, segmented centerlines; taxiways have continuous yellow centerlines. A student who is unsure which one they are on can use this [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(5)]].
Taxiway edge lights are blue; taxiway centerline lights are steady green [[33:133|AIM 2-1-10a]] [[33:133|AIM 2-1-10b]].
RWSL is an independent safety layer. It does not substitute for or convey an ATC clearance [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6a]].

callout.text: Teach it: known to unknown works well here [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Start with the hold marking the student sees every flight at home, then add the lights and signs that support it. The rule to drill is short: red sign or red light means stop until cleared, and solid lines face you means stop.

check.q: In fog, ground clears you across Runway 4, but the stop bar in front of you is still lit red. What do you do?
check.a: Stay stopped and contact ATC. Pilots should never cross a red illuminated stop bar, even with a clearance [[33:134|AIM 2-1-10e CAUTION]].

chunks.title: K5: Flight deck activities while taxiing: plan, brief hot spots, talk to ATC

body.p: Plan the surface movement like any other phase of flight, in two parts: review items and briefing items [[7:3|AC 91-73B 7b]]. The goal of a taxi SOP is to raise the pilot's awareness without adding workload while the airplane moves [[7:2|AC 91-73B 5b]].

head: Part
What to do
rows: Review: NOTAMs and ATIS
Look for runway and taxiway closures and construction. If cleared onto a surface a NOTAM or ATIS says is closed, query the controller [[7:3|AC 91-73B 7b(1)(c)]].
Review: diagram and hot spots
Get the big picture of where incursions could happen [[7:3|AC 91-73B 7b(1)(d)]].
Brief: route and hot spots
Expected route, hold short lines, runways to cross, hot spots and other conflicts. Review the route again once the real instructions arrive [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(d)]].
Brief: timing of tasks
Time checklists and radio calls so they do not interfere with watching the taxi; do checklists only when stopped or taxiing straight with no complex intersections [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(a)]].
Brief: critical locations
Hot spots, intervening runway crossings, entering and lining up on the runway, and lining up to land [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(f)]].
Brief: occupants
Sterile cockpit, but anyone who sees a conflict speaks up [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(b)]]. Phones and devices off during taxi [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(j)]].

body.p: Hot spots. A hot spot is a runway safety problem area or intersection, typically a complex or confusing taxiway/taxiway or taxiway/runway intersection, sometimes with a history of surface incidents [[2:124|Chart Users' Guide, Hot Spots]]. On the airport diagram it is a brown open circle or ellipse leadered to a number such as 'HS 1', and the number matches a description on the Hot Spot page in the front of the TPP [[2:124|Chart Users' Guide, Hot Spots]]. Before taxi, identify every hot spot in or near the route and brief it [[7:8|AC 91-73B 7g(1)]].

Communicating and coordinating with ATC. Do all high-workload, heads-down work such as GPS programming before the airplane moves; many errors happen when a pilot is off frequency or heads-down [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(3) NOTE]]. Focus on the clearance and do no nonessential tasks while talking to ATC [[7:8|AC 91-73B 7f(3)]]. Tell ATC whenever you do not understand a clearance [[7:8|AC 91-73B 7f]]. The tower may lose its radio at any time, so scan the tower while taxiing and on the runway for light signals [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(3)]].

callout.text: Teach it: AC 91-73B Appendix 2 is a ready-made pretaxi briefing card (ATC taxi clearance, taxi route and hot spots, any special considerations) [[7:15|AC 91-73B App 2]]. Have your student brief you from it, out loud, at the tie-down. That turns K5 into a habit you can grade.

check.q: Where on the airport diagram is a hot spot shown, and where is its description?
check.a: A brown open circle or ellipse leadered to a number like HS 1; the description is on the Hot Spot page in the front of the TPP [[2:124|Chart Users' Guide, Hot Spots]].

chunks.title: K6: Communication and procedures at uncontrolled airports

body.p: Without a tower, no one tells the pilot where to stop. The pilot must rely on signs, hold short lines, other markings, lighting and the airport diagram [[7:14|AC 91-73B App 1 para 3]]. Some aircraft have no radio, and some pilots do not announce, so alertness is essential [[33:205|AIM 4-1-9a]] [[7:14|AC 91-73B App 1 para 5]]. Many training flights happen at nontowered airports, which raises the need for vigilance [[24:34|AFH 1-13]].

head: Moment
Recommended call or action (AIM TBL 4-1-1)
rows: Leaving the parking area
Announce before taxiing [[33:207|AIM 4-1-9 TBL 4-1-1]].
At the departure runway
Announce before taxiing onto the runway for departure [[33:207|AIM 4-1-9 TBL 4-1-1]].
Inbound
Monitor and communicate from 10 miles to landing; report downwind, base and final [[33:207|AIM 4-1-9c]] [[33:207|AIM 4-1-9 TBL 4-1-1]].
After landing
Report leaving the runway [[33:207|AIM 4-1-9 TBL 4-1-1]].
Departing
Monitor from engine start, during taxi, and until 10 miles from the airport [[33:207|AIM 4-1-9c]].

bullets: Frequency: the CTAF may be a UNICOM, MULTICOM, FSS or tower frequency [[33:206|AIM 4-1-9b]]. With no tower, FSS or UNICOM, self-announce on MULTICOM 122.9 [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g]].
Say the airport name at the beginning and end of each self-announce call, use the runway number instead of 'active runway', and never say 'traffic in the area, please advise' [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g]].
Part-time tower: be certain of its status before operating; if in doubt, try calling on the tower frequency [[7:13|AC 91-73B App 1 para 2]].
Expect instrument approaches to a different runway, possibly one that crosses the VFR runway, or to the opposite end of the departure runway [[7:13|AC 91-73B App 1 para 2]].
Do not line up and hold on the departure runway any longer than absolutely necessary [[7:14|AC 91-73B App 1 para 5]].

Before entering or crossing a runway, listen on the CTAF and scan the full length of the runway and its approach and departure paths [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(12)]]. Taxi past the hold sign only when the runway is clear and no aircraft is on final [[1:342|PHAK 14-8]].

callout.text: Teach it: the AIH sample SBT lesson has the learner plan an arrival at a specific nontowered airport (wind, runways, communications, pattern) and then debrief what was done and why [[25:155|AIH 7-11]]. Extend that scenario to the ground: the taxi out, the runway crossing and the departure call.

check.q: Your student calls 'Mayfield traffic, any traffic in the area please advise.' What do you teach?
check.a: That phrase is not a recognized self-announce call and should not be used. State position and intentions, use the runway number, and say the airport name at the start and end [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g]].

chunks.title: R1: Distractions, task priority, lost awareness and disorientation

body.p: Situational awareness on the surface means knowing exactly where the aircraft is and running a 'continuous loop': confirm present position, then figure out the next point that needs extra attention, such as a turn, an intersecting runway or a hot spot [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7d]]. Distraction breaks that loop.

head: Hazard
Mitigation from the sources
rows: Distractions in the cabin

Ask passengers for a sterile cockpit from the start of preflight preparations until clear of the terminal area and at cruising altitude, and again from landing preparation until stopped at the parking spot [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7c]]. Phones and devices off [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(j)]].
Task prioritization

Complete checklist items (flaps, trim, GPS entries) before taxi [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(g)]]. Limit or eliminate non-ATC communications while moving [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(2)]]. On the ground you can always stop and resume after addressing an issue [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].
Loss of situational awareness
Keep the diagram out and in view at all times [[24:55|AFH 2-18]]; eyes outside, scanning side to side, near and far [[24:56|AFH 2-19]].
Disorientation

Never stop on a runway. Stop the aircraft, immediately advise ATC and, if needed, request progressive taxi [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(5)]] [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(7)]]. Tell the controller at the first sign of disorientation [[33:262|AIM 4-3-19]].

callout.text: You are a distraction too. AC 91-73B tells flight schools to have instructors limit cockpit instruction during taxi and to put a placard on the panel reminding them [[7:17|AC 91-73B App 3 para 2]]. The AIH adds that the instructor must model the sterile flight deck, not just teach it [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

Teach it: brief the lesson on the ground and save the teaching for the run-up area, which is stopped and off the taxiway. If something must be said while rolling, make it a short instruction, not a lecture.

check.q: Your student becomes unsure of position while crossing a wide runway intersection. Where should the airplane stop?
check.a: Not on a runway. Stop clear of runways, advise ATC immediately and request progressive taxi if needed [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(7)]] [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(5)]].

chunks.title: R2: Expectation and confirmation bias in taxi instructions

body.p: Expectation bias is a wrong assessment that persists despite evidence it is wrong [[30:45|RMH 6-2]]. It often happens while taxiing: pilots expect a particular route and hear the clearance as expected rather than as given, and pilots who routinely get the same clearance at a familiar airport are more susceptible [[30:46|RMH 6-3]]. The AFH warns that it only takes one missed instruction or turn to cause an accident [[24:56|AFH 2-19]].

Confirmation bias is a little different: the pilot suppresses information that does not fit the expectation instead of reacting to it. Either one, uncorrected, leads to an error, and fatigue makes both more likely [[30:45|RMH 6-2]] [[30:46|RMH 6-3]].

bullets: Planning itself sets expectations. Follow the clearance actually received, not the one you expected [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(e) CAUTION]].
Be especially vigilant when a similar call sign is on frequency, so you do not act on another aircraft's instruction [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(6)]] [[1:367|PHAK 14-33]].
Read back the complete clearance with your call sign; it gives ATC the chance to catch an error [[1:367|PHAK 14-33]].
Flight schools can reduce call sign confusion by having pilots say every digit, for example 'three-one-six', not 'three sixteen' [[7:17|AC 91-73B App 3 para 6]].

callout.text: Teach it: write down the clearance before reading it back, then read from the paper, not from memory. When the clearance differs from the brief, have the student say so out loud ('That is different from what we briefed'). On a familiar route, ask ground for a different route now and then (traffic permitting) so the student never learns to stop listening.

check.q: Which pilot does the RMH say is more susceptible to expectation bias while taxiing?
check.a: A pilot familiar with the airport who routinely receives the same taxi clearance [[30:46|RMH 6-3]].

body.p: Before entering or crossing any runway the pilot must be positive that ATC has cleared it. Scan the full length of the runway and the final approach; if the scan raises any doubt, stop and ask ATC [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(4)]]. The PHAK says to scan even if ATC has issued a clearance [[1:368|PHAK 14-34]]. Approaching a runway entrance, comply with the hold short or crossing clearance and come to a complete stop, or be in a phase of taxi with no incursion risk, before doing checklists [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(5)]].

head: Situation
Technique
rows: Crossing a runway
All exterior lights on [[7:10|AC 91-73B 7h(2)(c)]]. Cross in a timely manner [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(6)]].
Entering for takeoff or LUAW
All lights on except landing lights; strobes off if they would blind others [[7:10|AC 91-73B 7h(2)(d)]]. Scan the full runway and final, at the end or at an intersection [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(8)]].
LUAW with no reason given
Expect a call within 90 seconds; if none, call ATC [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(9)]]. LUAW is not a takeoff clearance [[1:368|PHAK 14-34]].
Lining up
Set the heading bug to the runway heading and check heading and runway agree before adding power, to avoid a wrong-runway departure [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].
Radio unusually quiet
Suspect a stuck microphone or radio problem; contact ATC and look for light gun signals [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(9) NOTE]].

body.p: Runway confusion is a subset of incursions: taking off or landing on a taxiway or wrong runway, usually without knowing it until after it happens. Three factors raise the risk: airport complexity, close proximity of runway thresholds, and joint use of a runway as a taxiway [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]]. When told to use a runway as a taxiway, do not take off on it [[1:367|PHAK 14-33]].

callout.text: Your clearance, not the lights, lets you enter. But red REL or THL lights mean the runway is unsafe: stop or stay stopped and contact ATC if they conflict with your clearance [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6b]] [[33:128|AIM 2-1-6c]].

check.q: Tower clears you to line up and wait, gives no reason, and two minutes pass in silence. What should have happened, and when?
check.a: With no reason given, expect a call within 90 seconds; if none comes, call ATC, and scan the tower for light signals [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(9)]] [[7:18|AC 91-73B App 3 para 9]].

body.p: Plan the exit before landing. While en route, after getting the ATIS, review the diagram and brief the exit taxiway, including any runway hold markings close to it [[1:369|PHAK 14-35]]. Use caution after landing on a runway that intersects another, or where the exit taxiway is close to another runway's hold short line [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(10)]].

bullets: Exit at the first available taxiway or as instructed. Do not exit onto another runway unless ATC authorizes it, and at a towered airport do not stop or reverse course on the runway without approval [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]].
Do not accept a last-minute turnoff instruction unless you clearly understand it and are certain you can safely comply [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(14)]].

You are clear of the runway only when all parts of the aircraft, including the tail, are past the runway holding position marking. Once past it, hold unless ATC has given more instructions [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]] [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(11)]].
No ATC clearance is needed to cross the hold marking when exiting; you will see the dashed lines first [[1:342|PHAK 14-8]] [[1:344|PHAK 14-10]].
Change nothing (flaps, trim, frequencies) until the whole aircraft has crossed the hold short line [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(g)]] [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(13)]].
Do not change from tower to ground until the controller directs it [[33:258|AIM 4-3-14]].

body.p: LAHSO adds a hold short point on the landing runway itself. Accepting 'cleared to land Runway 36, hold short of Runway 23' means you must exit before the hold marking or stop at it [[1:345|PHAK 14-11]]. LAHSO is not authorized for student pilots performing a solo flight [[1:345|PHAK 14-11]].

callout.text: Teach it: on every landing ask 'Where does the tail have to be?' until the student says it before you can ask. Students who clean up on the rollout learned it from an instructor who did; keep your own hands off the flaps until the airplane is clear.

check.q: After landing, ATC has not given further instructions. How far must the student taxi, and then what?
check.a: Until every part of the aircraft is past the landing runway's holding position marking, then hold unless ATC has issued more instructions [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]].

chunks.title: R7: Operating on taxiways between parallel runways

body.p: AC 91-73B cautions pilots to use increased awareness when taxiing between active parallel runways [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(5) CAUTION]]. The space is short: after exiting one runway, the next runway's hold line may be only a few airplane lengths away.

head: Trap
What the sources say
rows: Boxed in after landing

If an adjacent parallel runway's hold short line keeps you from clearing the landing runway, stop and immediately advise ATC [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(11)]]. Without instructions, you may protrude into or cross another taxiway or ramp to get past the hold markings [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]], but never another runway.
Similar-sounding names

Airport designers give entrance taxiways different designations (for example C6 and D6) because the same name at both runways is hazardous and similar to runway names like 18L and 18C [[19:23|AC 150/5340-18H 1.4.6]].
Multiple crossings close together
ATC normally issues one runway crossing at a time, but exceptions may apply to closely spaced runways less than 1,000 feet apart [[1:368|PHAK 14-34]].
Two departure ends close together
Use the compass or heading display to confirm the runway, especially where departure ends of two runways are close [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(1)]].
Short taxiway, shortened cues
On a taxiway joining closely spaced runways, the enhanced centerline dashes may stop at the runway edge instead of running the full 150 feet [[20:76|AC 150/5340-1M 4.3.4.1]].

callout.text: Teach it: on the diagram, have the student name every hold line between the landing runway and the ramp before the approach. Between parallels, the briefing sounds like: 'Exit at Charlie, stop past the 27R hold line, expect to hold short of 27L.'

check.q: You exit Runway 27R and the 27L hold line is so close that your tail is still over the 27R hold markings. What do you do?
check.a: Stop and immediately advise ATC. Do not cross the 27L hold line without a clearance [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(11)]].

chunks.title: R4 and R5: Night and low-visibility taxi

body.p: Night taxi operations (R4). Taxiing at an unfamiliar airport is harder at night and in low visibility [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]]. Before taxi at night, check the ramp with a flashlight; obstructions that are easy to see by day are hard to see at night [[24:225|AFH 11-8]]. Taxi slowly with the taxi or landing light on (watch for overheating and for blinding others), follow the painted lines, and confirm that the position, route and runway all look as expected; if anything conflicts, do not continue the taxi or the takeoff [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].

bullets: Hold or lock the brakes during the night run-up; the airplane can creep forward unnoticed [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].
Position lights are required on the surface from sunset to sunrise; turn on navigation, position and anti-collision lights before taxi [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]].
At night when cleared to LUAW, consider lining up about 3 feet left or right of the centerline so a landing pilot can tell you apart from the runway lights [[7:10|AC 91-73B 7h(2)(e)]].
Be especially vigilant on LUAW at night or in reduced visibility [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(9)]].

body.p: Low visibility taxi operations (R5). Low visibility increases runway incursion risk, so use every resource: the diagram, the heading indicator, and the signs, markings and lights. Do heads-down tasks only while stopped [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(4)]]. In some low-visibility conditions the tower cannot see you, so it cannot visually confirm you are following instructions [[33:262|AIM 4-3-19]].

head: Low visibility item
Source
rows: Brief the low visibility taxi chart if one is published, and listen for 'hold short of the ILS critical area'
Tell the controller at the first sign of disorientation; use extreme caution taxiing toward the sun
Low visibility taxi plans (LVOSMGCS) apply below 1,200 ft RVR, at two levels: below 1,200 to 500 ft RVR, and below 500 ft RVR
Withhold checklists and nonessential talk until the aircraft is stopped and the brakes set
Never cross a red stop bar, even when cleared
Standard taxi routes are not requested or issued during low visibility SMGCS operations

callout.text: Teaching risk: the first night or low-visibility taxi is a poor time to also teach a new radio skill. Build the night taxi on day habits the student already owns, one new element at a time (simple to complex) [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

check.q: In low visibility, when may your student run the before-takeoff checklist?
check.a: Only when the aircraft is stopped with the brakes set; while moving, full attention goes to taxiing [[33:262|AIM 4-3-19]] [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(4)]].

body.p: AC 91-73B says taxi SOPs should be emphasized in certification and proficiency training, used in every phase including ground operations, and evaluated on every flight review [[7:3|AC 91-73B 6]]. For a skill like taxiing, the demonstration-performance method fits: explanation, demonstration, learner performance with instructor supervision, and evaluation [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. The explanation phase belongs on the ground, before the flight [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

head: Phase
What you do for runway incursion avoidance
rows: Explanation (ground)
Diagram, hot spots, NOTAMs, the expected clearance, hold lines and the 'stop if unsure' rule. Invite questions [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].
Instructor tells, instructor does
You make the calls, write the clearance, read it back and taxi, explaining each step as you do it, exactly the way the student will [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
Learner tells, instructor does
The student tells you what to write, read back, and where to stop while you taxi; you hear their understanding [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
Learner tells, learner does
The student taxis and talks through it ('next is the Runway 31 hold line, we hold short'); you watch for faulty habits and correct them early [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
Evaluation
Collaborative assessment: the student self-assesses first, then you compare with your assessment [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

body.p: Then move to scenario-based training. SBT puts maneuvers into realistic scenarios to build decision making, and the instructor shifts from teacher to mentor once the learner starts making decisions [[25:154|AIH 7-10]] [[25:155|AIH 7-11]]. Scenarios that fit this Task: a route change from ground, a NOTAM-closed taxiway, a part-time tower that just closed, a night arrival between parallel runways.

bullets: AC 91-73B Appendix 3 best practices for schools and CFIs: monthly recurrent training with an online runway safety course, the same course for students before first solo [[7:17|AC 91-73B App 3 para 4]].
Tower visits for new CFIs to discuss incursion avoidance with ATC [[7:17|AC 91-73B App 3 para 5]].
Consider having students announce 'Student Pilot' with the school call sign, and scheduling flights at low-traffic times [[7:17|AC 91-73B App 3 para 7]] [[7:17|AC 91-73B App 3 para 8]].
Teach students that, if not cleared to land on final, they ask the tower 'am I cleared to land?' and go around if there is no answer [[7:18|AC 91-73B App 3 para 10]].

callout.text: On the CFI practical test this is a knowledge Task you teach on the ground. Bring an airport diagram with hot spots, a sample clearance to write out, and one scenario per risk element, and deliver it as a lesson, not a list.

check.q: AC 91-73B Appendix 3 suggests one visit for every new CFI. Where, and why?
check.a: A tower visit, built into the CFI standardization syllabus, to discuss runway incursion avoidance procedures with ATC personnel [[7:17|AC 91-73B App 3 para 5]].

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Weak hold short readback
'Roger' or a readback with no runway number
Call sign, runway designator and 'hold short' every time; no Roger or Wilco [[7:8|AC 91-73B 7f(4)]] [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18a9]].
Reading back the expected route
Readback matches the usual route, not the one given
Write it first, read from the paper, follow what was received [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(e) CAUTION]] [[24:56|AFH 2-19]].
Heads-down while rolling
Programming the GPS or reading the checklist while moving
Do high-workload tasks before taxi; checklists only when stopped or straight ahead [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(3) NOTE]] [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(a)]].
Creeping over the hold line
Nose or wheel over the solid lines
Stop with no part of the aircraft past the marking [[33:151|AIM 2-3-5a]]; use a reminder object on a knob or the yoke [[7:8|AC 91-73B 7f(3)]].
Stopping on a runway when lost
Student stops on, or keeps rolling across, a runway while unsure
Never stop on a runway; stop clear, advise ATC, ask for progressive taxi [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(7)]] [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(5)]].
Crossing without a scan
Crosses the moment cleared, eyes inside
Scan the full length and the final even when cleared; lights on [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(4)]] [[1:368|PHAK 14-34]].
Tail over the hold line after landing
Stops just off the runway edge
Taxi until the whole aircraft, tail included, is past the hold line [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(11)]].
Cleaning up on the runway
Flaps up or frequency change during rollout
Nothing nonessential until clear of all runways [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(13)]].
Vague CTAF calls
'Traffic in the area, please advise', no airport name, 'active runway'
Airport name first and last, runway number, position and intentions [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g]].
Instructor over-talking during taxi
Long explanations while the student taxis
Limit cockpit instruction during taxi; teach at the run-up area; model the sterile flight deck [[7:17|AC 91-73B App 3 para 2]] [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

body.p: When you point out an error, offer a concrete fix and try not to end the evaluation on a negative note [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. If the student cannot reach the standard in the time you planned, schedule more training rather than signing off [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

check.q: Your student uses a sticky note on the yoke after reading back 'hold short Runway 31'. Is that a recognized technique?
check.a: Yes. AC 91-73B suggests placing something on a knob, the panel, the compass or the yoke as a reminder to hold short [[7:8|AC 91-73B 7f(3)]].

chunks.title: Reading the chart: the airport diagram and its hot spots

body.p: The airport diagram is a taxi tool. The FAA designs it to help with ground movement at airports with complex runway and taxiway layouts; it is not intended for approach, landing or departure operations, and it helps a pilot identify his or her location, which reduces requests for progressive taxi instructions [[2:122|Chart Users' Guide p 122]]. Teach the student to study it before engine start and to trace the route he expects, then compare it with the clearance he actually gets.

Show the three features that matter most for incursion avoidance. A hot spot is a brown circle or ellipse with a leader to a number such as HS 1; it marks a complex or confusing intersection that may have a history of surface incidents [[2:124|Chart Users' Guide p 124]]. Hold lines are on the diagram too: land and hold short lines and ILS hold lines with their critical areas [[2:123|Chart Users' Guide p 123]]. And the sample diagram's caution note says to be alert to runway crossing clearances and that readback of all runway holding instructions is required [[2:123|Chart Users' Guide p 123]].

Teach the construction symbols as a short list. A hard surface is solid; other than hard surface is a dot pattern; a closed runway has an X at each end; a surface under construction is outlined with dots; stopways, overruns and blast pads show a chevron pattern [[2:124|Chart Users' Guide p 124]]. The most common misread is to see gray and think 'taxiway'. Gray with chevrons is not a taxi route. The description of each hot spot is on the Hot Spot page at the front of the Terminal Procedures Publication [[2:124|Chart Users' Guide p 124]].

Finish with the rule the diagram supports. At a towered airport, no one may operate on a runway or taxiway, or take off or land, without the appropriate clearance [[60:454|14 CFR 91.129(i)]]. The diagram helps a student know where he is; it does not give him permission to move.

scenario.title: Pre-solo student, busy towered field, fog lifting
scenario.setup: Your pre-solo student has 14 hours, all from this towered airport. It has parallel Runways 27L and 27R, a crossing runway, and one hot spot (HS 1) where a taxiway meets both 27L and the crossing runway. Morning fog is lifting; the ATIS reports a taxiway closed for construction. The school ramp is north of 27R, and the run-up area for 27L is between the two runways, next to the 27L hold line. The student usually taxis via Alpha.

questions.q: What should the student review and brief before you start the engine?
questions.a: NOTAMs and ATIS for closures (query ATC if cleared onto a closed taxiway), the current diagram and hot spots for the big picture [[7:3|AC 91-73B 7b(1)(c)]] [[7:3|AC 91-73B 7b(1)(d)]], and a briefing of the expected route, hold lines, runway crossings and hot spots, plus when checklists will be done [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(a)]] [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(d)]].

questions.q: Ground gives 'Runway 27L, taxi via Bravo, hold short of Runway 27R.' The student reads back 'via Alpha, hold short 27R'. What is going on, and what do you do?
questions.a: Expectation bias: a pilot who routinely gets the same clearance hears the expected one [[30:46|RMH 6-3]]. Have the student correct the readback from a written copy; follow the clearance actually received, not the expected one [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(e) CAUTION]] [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7e]].

questions.q: Rolling toward HS 1 the student starts loading the GPS flight plan. What do you say and why?
questions.a: Stop that task or stop the airplane. High-workload heads-down work belongs before taxi, and checklists are done stopped or on a straight taxiway without complex intersections [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(3) NOTE]] [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(a)]]. A hot spot is exactly where enhanced vigilance is needed [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(f)]].

questions.q: At the 27R hold line ground says 'cross Runway 27R'. Stop bars are not in use. What does the student do before and during the crossing?
questions.a: Be positive the clearance is for you, scan the full length of 27R and its final, and stop and ask ATC if anything is unclear [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(4)]]. Turn on all exterior lights and cross without delay [[7:10|AC 91-73B 7h(2)(c)]] [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(6)]]. Now the airplane is between parallel runways, so expect the 27L hold line soon [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(5) CAUTION]].

questions.q: Fog thickens; the student is no longer sure which taxiway they are on and slows to a stop with the nose wheel on a runway. What is the correct response?
questions.a: Never stop on a runway: clear it (if safe and clear of conflict) or as ATC directs, then stop and immediately advise ATC and request progressive taxi [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(7)]] [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(5)]]. In low visibility the tower may not be able to see you, so the call matters [[33:262|AIM 4-3-19]].

questions.q: After the flight, how do you debrief this so it sticks?
questions.a: Use collaborative assessment: the student self-assesses first, then you compare it with your assessment [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. Then rebuild the taxi as a scenario for the next lesson with a different route change [[25:155|AIH 7-11]], and consider the runway safety course required before first solo in AC 91-73B best practices [[7:17|AC 91-73B App 3 para 4]].

skills.do: The examiner will have you "Deliver instruction on the elements and techniques for runway incursion avoidance" (ACS AI.II.C.S1). Expect to teach a short ground lesson using an airport diagram: define a runway incursion, show how to write and read back a clearance, brief hot spots, explain hold lines and the lights that protect them, cover nontowered procedures, and explain how you would manage each risk element (bias, distraction, crossings, night, low visibility, after landing, parallel runways) with a student, including common student errors and how you fix them.
skills.practice: Pick a towered airport with published hot spots. Write a 10-minute lesson plan using demonstration-performance [[25:175|AIH 9-5]], with a sample clearance written in AC 91-73B shorthand [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7e(2)]] and the Appendix 2 pretaxi briefing card [[7:15|AC 91-73B App 2]]. Teach it to another instructor applicant, have them play a student who reads back the expected route, and practice correcting it.

quiz.q: Your school's call sign is 'Eagle 316.' What does AC 91-73B Appendix 3 suggest for how students say it?
options: 'Eagle three sixteen,' the shorter form ATC prefers
Only the last two digits once ATC has used them
Every digit: 'Eagle three-one-six'
'Eagle three sixteen, student,' but only on the CTAF
quiz.why: Appendix 3 suggests a school call sign format that requires saying every digit, for example 'three-one-six' rather than 'three sixteen', to cut call sign confusion [[7:17|AC 91-73B App 3 para 6]].

quiz.q: Which word will ATC not use when authorizing an aircraft to taxi?
options: Hold short
Via
Cleared
Cross
quiz.why: To prevent misunderstandings, ATC will not use the word 'cleared' with taxi authorization [[33:260|AIM 4-3-18a]].

quiz.q: In AC 91-73B written-taxi shorthand, what does an 'X' mean?
options: Cross
Hold short
Closed taxiway
Clearance limit
quiz.why: The AC's symbols are '/' for hold short and 'X' for cross [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7e(2)]].

quiz.q: Your student has just landed and cleared the runway. When should she switch from tower to ground?
options: As soon as all parts of the airplane are past the hold line
Once she stops and finishes the after-landing flow
Right after touchdown, so ground can plan the taxi route
Only when the tower controller directs her to
quiz.why: A pilot who has just landed should not change from the tower frequency to the ground control frequency until directed to do so by the controller [[33:258|AIM 4-3-14]].

quiz.q: After landing, with no ATC instructions, the only way past the hold markings puts your nose into a parallel taxiway. What does the AIM expect?
options: Stop on the runway and wait for the tower to give an exit
Turn onto the next runway ahead, since that is the shortest way clear
Back-taxi on the runway to an exit with more room behind the line
Taxi past the hold markings, even into the other taxiway, then hold
quiz.why: Without ATC instructions the pilot is expected to taxi beyond the landing runway's holding position markings, even if that means protruding into or crossing another taxiway or ramp area, then hold. Do not exit onto another runway, or stop or reverse on the runway, without ATC approval [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]].

quiz.q: Fog brings low visibility SMGCS operations. Your student wants to ask ground for the standard taxi route she knows well. What does the AIM say?
options: Do not request one; ATC may not issue STRs during low visibility SMGCS
Request it, since an STR is the simplest clearance in low visibility
Request it, but only with progressive taxi added to the route
Ask for it by name, since a route she knows needs no diagram review
quiz.why: Pilots should not request, and ATC may not issue, STR instructions during low visibility SMGCS operations [[33:263|AIM 4-3-20]].

quiz.q: What does AC 91-73B Appendix 3 tell flight schools about instructors and taxiing?
options: Do all of the taxiing for pre-solo students, until the student is ready for first solo
Limit cockpit instruction during taxi, with a panel placard as a reminder
Brief the lesson while taxiing, to save Hobbs time on the ground
Keep the radio on intercom only, so the student hears no ATC calls
quiz.why: Instructors should limit cockpit instruction during critical phases, particularly taxi, and placards should remind them [[7:17|AC 91-73B App 3 para 2]].

quiz.q: Under AC 91-73B Appendix 3, when should a school's students complete the online runway safety course?
options: Before the private pilot checkride, as part of the endorsement
Only after they cause a runway incursion or pilot deviation
Before the first cross-country, when they leave the home airport
As part of initial ground school, before their first solo
quiz.why: Appendix 3: school CFIs do monthly recurrent training that includes an online runway safety course, and students take it as part of initial ground school and complete it before their first solo [[7:17|AC 91-73B App 3 para 4]].

quiz.q: On a short taxiway joining two closely spaced runways, your student sees the enhanced centerline dashes end at the runway edge, shorter than usual. Why?
options: The taxiway is closed beyond that point, so stop at the dashes
The dashes are worn out and the airport must repaint the full 150 ft
Each enhancement ends at the runway edge if the full 150 ft will not fit
It marks an ILS critical area, so hold there if ATC instructs
quiz.why: On a taxiway serving two closely spaced runways, each enhancement terminates at the runway edge unless the full 150 ft can be painted [[20:76|AC 150/5340-1M 4.3.4.1]]. The holding position marking still means stop without a clearance [[33:151|AIM 2-3-5a]].

quiz.q: At night, cleared to line up and wait, what lining-up technique does AC 91-73B suggest?
options: Line up about 3 feet left or right of centerline
Line up exactly on the centerline lights
Stop at the threshold bars, short of the runway numbers
Turn off all lights so you do not blind landing traffic
quiz.why: Consider lining up about 3 feet left or right of the centerline so a landing aircraft can tell you apart from the runway lights [[7:10|AC 91-73B 7h(2)(e)]].

quiz.q: On the sample airport diagram, a brown circle with a leader to a box labelled 'HS 1' surrounds the point where two runways cross. What does it mark?
options: A radio frequency change point where pilots call ground control
The position of the control tower and its blind spots
A runway safety hot spot, usually a confusing intersection
A helicopter landing pad with its own approach path
quiz.why: Hot spots are indicated by a brown open circle or ellipse leadered to a Hot Spot number, and mark a runway-safety problem area or intersection [[2:124|Chart Users' Guide p 124]].

quiz.q: The sample diagram carries the note 'CAUTION: BE ALERT TO RUNWAY CROSSING CLEARANCES. READBACK OF ALL RUNWAY HOLDING INSTRUCTIONS IS REQUIRED.' What does the note ask for?
options: A readback only for clearances to cross runways
A readback of all runway holding instructions
A readback only when the tower is closed
No readback if the hold line is in sight
quiz.why: The diagram's own caution note says readback of all runway holding instructions is required [[2:123|Chart Users' Guide p 123]].

quiz.q: Next to 'AIRPORT TOWER' on the diagram's frequency list is a star. What do you teach your student?
options: The tower is part-time; see the Chart Supplement for hours
The tower frequency is reserved for military aircraft only
The tower has been permanently closed and removed
The tower provides radar approach control service
quiz.why: A star in the comm frequencies indicates part-time status, and the pilot should check the Chart Supplement for times of operation [[2:123|Chart Users' Guide p 123]].

quiz.q: A student sees a runway outline with an X at each end on an airport diagram. What does it mean?
options: Displaced threshold
Under construction
A stopway or overrun
Closed runway
quiz.why: The legend names the outline with an X at each end as a closed runway [[2:124|Chart Users' Guide p 124]].

quiz.q: Your student is cleared to taxi from the ramp at a towered airport. Which operation needs an appropriate ATC clearance?
options: Only takeoff, landing, and crossing a runway
Only operating on a runway, including crossing one
Runway or taxiway operation, takeoff, or landing
None until she reaches the first runway hold line
quiz.why: At an airport with an operating control tower, no person may operate an aircraft on a runway or taxiway, or take off or land, without an appropriate ATC clearance [[60:454|14 CFR 91.129(i)]].

final_quiz.q: Your student taxis at a part-time towered airport at 2215. The tower closed at 2200, but the student calls 'tower' twice and hears nothing. What does AC 91-73B Appendix 1 say a pilot should do about tower status?
options: Assume it is still open and hold short of the runway until a light gun signal comes from the cab
Be certain of the tower's status before operating; if in doubt, try the tower frequency
Taxi onto the runway and wait there for a steady green light from the tower
Use 121.5 to ask any station whether the tower is still open tonight
final_quiz.why: Pilots must be absolutely certain of a part-time tower's status before operating; if in doubt, attempt contact on the tower's frequency [[7:13|AC 91-73B App 1 para 2]].

final_quiz.q: The part-time tower has closed and your student plans a VFR departure on Runway 9 in a light breeze. What should you add to the taxi brief?
options: Nothing; with the tower closed, every pilot will use Runway 9
IFR arrivals may use another runway, even one crossing 9, or the opposite end
Instrument arrivals can only use Runway 9 once the tower is closed
Self-announce on the ATIS frequency so arriving IFR traffic hears you
final_quiz.why: Aircraft may be flying an instrument approach to a runway other than the VFR runway in use; it may intersect the VFR runway, or an instrument arrival may come to the opposite end of the departure runway [[7:13|AC 91-73B App 1 para 2b(2)]].

final_quiz.q: Taxiing at an unfamiliar airport, what 'continuous loop' does AC 91-73B describe for keeping situational awareness?
options: Read the clearance back once every minute until reaching the runway
Check the gauges, then the diagram, then outside, in a fixed cycle
Know where you are now, and work out the next point that needs extra care
Call ground at each intersection to confirm where you are on the route
final_quiz.why: Pilots use a continuous loop: know the aircraft's present location and mentally work out the next location on the route that needs increased attention, such as a turn, an intersecting runway or a hot spot [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7d]].

final_quiz.q: Ground gives you a standard taxi route by name. Your route crosses Runway 4. What does the STR authorize?
options: Nothing about Runway 4; an STR never constitutes or implies a crossing clearance
Crossing Runway 4, because the crossing is part of the published route
Crossing Runway 4 only if it is inactive or closed at the time
Crossing Runway 4 after a 10-second scan of both approach paths
final_quiz.why: An STR instruction does not constitute nor imply a clearance to cross a runway [[33:263|AIM 4-3-20]].

final_quiz.q: Your student asks why the airport painted entrance taxiways 'C6' and 'D6' instead of calling both 'C6' at parallel Runways 18L and 18C. What do you answer?
options: It is a random choice by the airport sponsor, with no safety reason behind the names at all
The same name at both runways is hazardous and is easily confused with runway names
The letters show which of the two runways is longer and which is shorter
The numbers show the distance to the threshold in thousands of feet
final_quiz.why: Using the same designation for both intersections is hazardous and may confuse pilots; distinct names separate them from similar runway designators like 18L and 18C [[19:23|AC 150/5340-18H 1.4.6]].

final_quiz.q: Ground tells your student to taxi to Runway 31 via Runway 4, using it as a taxiway. What does the PHAK warn about?
options: Runway 4 is closed to all aircraft, so ask ground for another route
A runway used as a taxiway needs no scan, since ATC has closed it
Do not get confused and take off on the runway used as a taxiway
Use the landing light only, since the runway lights are off for taxi use
final_quiz.why: When instructed to use a runway as a taxiway, do not become confused and take off on the runway you are using as a taxiway [[1:367|PHAK 14-33]].

final_quiz.q: Which readback best meets AIM and AC 91-73B guidance for 'N4GW, Runway 36, taxi via Alpha, hold short of Runway 9'?
options: 'N4GW, Runway 36 via Alpha, hold short of Runway 9'
'Wilco, N4GW, taxi via Alpha to the runway'
'Roger, Runway 36 via Alpha, hold short, N4GW'
'Runway 36 via Alpha, hold short of Runway 9, thanks'
final_quiz.why: Read back the runway assignment and any hold short with the complete call sign and runway designator; avoid Roger or Wilco [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18a9]] [[7:8|AC 91-73B 7f(4)]].

final_quiz.q: At a nontowered airport after landing, your student wants to cross the parallel runway to reach the fuel pumps. What does AC 91-73B add beyond looking at the runway?
options: Nothing more; a good look up and down the runway is all that is needed
Call ground control on the CTAF and get a crossing clearance first
Listen on the CTAF and scan the final and departure paths too, since not all aircraft have radios
Ask the UNICOM operator to approve the crossing and to confirm that no aircraft is on the final approach
final_quiz.why: Not all aircraft are radio equipped; listen on the CTAF and scan the full runway plus its final approach and departure paths before entering or crossing [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(12)]].

final_quiz.q: You brief a student on LAHSO before their first solo at a field that uses it. What is true?
options: LAHSO is not authorized for student pilots performing a solo flight
Solo students must accept LAHSO when offered, to keep traffic moving
Students may accept LAHSO only at night, when traffic is lighter
LAHSO applies only to taxiways, so it does not affect the landing
final_quiz.why: LAHSO is not authorized for student pilots on solo flights [[1:345|PHAK 14-11]].

final_quiz.q: A flight review pilot taxis perfectly but never refers to the airport diagram. Under AC 91-73B, why should you address it on the review?
options: Taxi SOPs are not part of a flight review, which covers only flight maneuvers
The diagram is required by 61.56, so the review cannot be signed without it
Only student pilots need airport diagrams, so it is not worth mentioning
The AC says taxi SOP use should be evaluated on the flight review of every pilot
final_quiz.why: SOP use should be evaluated during the flight review under 61.56 [[7:3|AC 91-73B 6]], and CFIs should require pilots to have and use current airport diagrams [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2) NOTE]].

final_quiz.q: You are holding in position on Runway 27 at an intersection at night. Radios have been silent for a long time. What does AC 91-73B suggest?
options: Begin the takeoff roll, since a long silence means there is no traffic
Suspect a radio problem or stuck mic, call ATC and look for light signals
Exit the runway at the next taxiway without telling anyone, to stay safe
Turn on the landing lights and keep waiting for as long as the tower takes
final_quiz.why: If communications are unusually quiet, suspect radio problems or a stuck microphone, contact ATC and look for light gun signals [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(9) NOTE]].

final_quiz.q: Your student asks below what RVR an airport's low visibility taxi plan (LVOSMGCS) applies. What does the AIM say?
options: Below 2,400 ft RVR, at a single level for all operations
Below 1,800 ft RVR, at three levels that each airport sets
Below 600 ft RVR, and only when the tower cannot see the airplane
Below 1,200 ft RVR, at two levels: 1,200 to 500 and below 500
final_quiz.why: AC 120-57 (LVOSMGCS) describes a low visibility taxi plan for airports with operations below 1,200 ft RVR, at two levels: less than 1,200 to 500 ft RVR, and less than 500 ft RVR [[33:262|AIM 4-3-19]].

final_quiz.q: Why does the AIM say the runway holding position marking matters even for an airplane exiting the runway?
options: It shows where the exiting airplane must call ground control
It generally marks the boundary of the runway safety area
It marks where an exiting airplane waits for a crossing clearance
It marks the end of the landing distance available for LAHSO
final_quiz.why: Runway holding position markings generally also identify the boundary of the runway safety area for aircraft exiting the runway [[33:151|AIM 2-3-5a]]; no ATC clearance is needed to cross them when exiting [[1:342|PHAK 14-8]].

final_quiz.q: The sample diagram says 'ASDE-X in use' and asks pilots to operate transponders 'with altitude reporting mode and ADS-B (if equipped)' enabled. When?
options: On all airport surfaces
Only after takeoff roll begins
Only on the active runway
Only during night operations
final_quiz.why: The diagram's note says to operate transponders with altitude reporting mode and ADS-B (if equipped) enabled on all airport surfaces [[2:123|Chart Users' Guide p 123]].

final_quiz.q: At the end of Runway 6 on the sample diagram a dashed box carries the labels 'ILS HOLD' and 'ILS CRITICAL AREA'. What does it show?
options: A displaced threshold with its landing area
A closed pavement area under construction
A helicopter pad with its approach path
The ILS critical area and its hold position
final_quiz.why: The diagram's runway features include ILS hold lines and localizer and glide slope critical areas [[2:123|Chart Users' Guide p 123]].

final_quiz.q: Your student wants to know where to read the full description of a hot spot such as HS 1. Where is it?
options: In the sectional chart legend under airport symbols
In the Chart Supplement airport remarks section only
On the Hot Spot page of the Terminal Procedures Publication
In the notes on the back of the airport diagram
final_quiz.why: The hot spot number corresponds to a listing and description on the Hot Spot page in the front of the Terminal Procedures Publication [[2:124|Chart Users' Guide p 124]].

final_quiz.q: Ground tells your student to hold short of Runway 17. The runway looks clear and he starts to cross. What does the regulation say?
options: He may cross if the runway looks clear and no traffic is in sight nearby
No one may operate contrary to an ATC instruction, except in an emergency
He may cross if he reads the instruction back and then looks for traffic
He may cross if the tower has not repeated its instruction for 2 minutes
final_quiz.why: Except in an emergency, no person may operate an aircraft contrary to an ATC instruction in an area in which air traffic control is exercised [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(b)]].

takeaways: A runway incursion is any incorrect presence on a runway's protected area; no near miss is needed.
Every runway crossing needs its own explicit clearance; a taxi route never includes one.
Write the clearance, read back runway and hold short from the paper, trace it on the diagram.
Brief the route, hot spots and checklist timing before the airplane moves; heads-down work happens stopped.
Red sign, red stop bar or red RWSL light: stop and talk to ATC.
After landing the whole airplane, tail included, must pass the hold line; between parallels, stop and tell ATC if boxed in.
Teach it with demonstration-performance, then scenarios, and model the sterile flight deck yourself.
cfi_notes: The sources disagree on the definition. The PHAK and AFH use the older wording that requires a collision hazard or loss of separation [[1:365|PHAK 14-31]] [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]. AC 91-73B, which the ACS lists as a reference, quotes FAA Order 7050.1: incorrect presence on the protected area [[7:1|AC 91-73B 1]]. Teach the AC 91-73B wording and point out the older one so the student is not confused.

PHAK 14-36 says do not initiate non-essential communications or actions 'until the aircraft has stopped and the brakes set' after exiting [[1:370|PHAK 14-36]], while AC 91-73B ties it to being clear of all runways [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(13)]]. The AIM uses the 'stopped and the brakes set' wording only for low visibility taxi [[33:262|AIM 4-3-19]]. Teach the AC 91-73B standard (nothing nonessential until clear of all runways), the AIM rule in low visibility, and the habit of stopping before any heads-down task.

The PHAK lists 'turn on aircraft lights and the rotating beacon or strobe lights while taxiing' [[1:365|PHAK 14-31]], but AC 91-73B and the AIM say strobes should not be on during taxi if they would affect others' vision [[7:10|AC 91-73B 7h(2)(b)]] [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]]. Teach the AIM wording.

AC 91-73B mentions TCAS/TAS and FMS scratchpads [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(8)]] [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7e(1)]]. In a basic trainer, translate that to whatever traffic display the airplane has (ADS-B In on a tablet, for example) and to a kneeboard for the clearance; that translation is application, not source text.
Use the Appendix 2 pretaxi briefing card as a graded item from the first lesson [[7:15|AC 91-73B App 2]]; students who brief out loud early keep doing it.
When a student misreads a clearance, separate misconception from motor skill: having them talk through the taxi (learner tells, learner does) shows you which one it is [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
AC 91-73B is dated 7/30/12 and some of its web links are old [[7:2|AC 91-73B 4c]]; check the FAA Runway Safety pages for current hot spot and runway safety material before teaching from it.

The AIM uses 'hot spot' for a location with a history of potential risk of collision or incursion [[34:358|AIM P/C Glossary H-3]]; the Chart Users' Guide adds that it is typically a complex or confusing intersection [[2:124|Chart Users' Guide, Hot Spots]]. Students should read the HS descriptions in the TPP, not just see the circles.
Students learn more from what you do than what you say; if you change frequencies on the rollout, they will too [[25:164|AIH 8-6]].
gaps: The sources do not give hot spot descriptions for any particular airport; read the Hot Spot page in the front of the current TPP for the airports you teach at.
No source gives a step-by-step light setup for a specific trainer; exterior light use is limited by the AFM/POH and equipment, which AC 91-73B says to follow [[7:10|AC 91-73B 7h(2)]].

Local movement and non-movement area boundaries, a flight school letter of authorization with the tower and flight school call sign formats are set locally; the sources only say they exist [[33:260|AIM 4-3-18a]] [[7:17|AC 91-73B App 3 para 6]].
The sources do not say how a CFI should time a 'surprise' route change for training; coordinate any such exercise with ATC (a tower visit is a good place to ask) [[7:17|AC 91-73B App 3 para 5]].
Low visibility taxi charts and SMGCS procedures are airport specific; none is reproduced here, so brief from the actual chart if one is published [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(i)]].

activities.title: True or false: what a clearance does and does not allow
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: 'Runway 27, taxi via Alpha' lets you cross Runway 27 at any point on the way.
cards.why: False. It does not authorize entering or crossing the assigned departure runway at any point [[33:260|AIM 4-3-18a]].

cards.s: ATC normally issues crossing clearances one runway at a time.
cards.why: True. You must have crossed the previous runway before the next crossing is issued, with possible exceptions for runways less than 1,000 feet apart [[1:368|PHAK 14-34]].

cards.s: Ground's taxi clearance to parking after landing includes any runway on the way.
cards.why: False. It does not authorize entering or crossing any runway [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]].

cards.s: Controllers must ask for a readback of a hold short instruction if the pilot does not give one.
cards.why: True. Controllers are required to request it when it is not received [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18a]].

cards.s: If you cannot safely comply with a taxi instruction, the correct word is 'unable'.
cards.why: True. Inform ATC immediately using the word 'UNABLE' [[1:367|PHAK 14-33]].

cards.s: Accepting a standard taxi route means you are telling ATC you are fully familiar with it.
cards.why: True. By requesting an STR a pilot acknowledges full familiarity with it [[33:263|AIM 4-3-20]].

activities.title: Landing between parallels: one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are flying dual with a student into a towered airport with parallel Runways 27L and 27R. You are landing on 27R; the ramp is south of 27L.

steps.s: On a fast short final, tower says 'turn left at Charlie two if able.' Charlie two is close.
options: Brake hard to make Charlie two
Make Charlie two at any speed, then explain
Stop on the runway and ask for new instructions
Tell tower unable and plan the next taxiway you can safely make
steps.why: Do not accept a last-minute turnoff unless you can safely comply [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(14)]], and do not stop on the runway at a towered airport without approval [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]].

steps.s: You exit at Charlie three. Your tail just clears the 27R hold line, and the 27L hold line is right ahead. The student reaches for the flaps and the ground frequency.
options: Let the student retract the flaps now, since the airplane is already clear of the landing runway
Stop past the 27R hold line, short of 27L, no flap or frequency changes, and wait for tower
Continue across 27L to the ramp, since tower said to exit and the crossing is the obvious next step
Switch to ground now and request the crossing, since the tail is clear of the 27R hold line
steps.why: Hold once past the landing runway's hold markings unless instructed [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]]; nonessential actions wait until clear of all runways [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(13)]]; change to ground only when tower directs [[33:258|AIM 4-3-14]].

steps.s: Tower: 'contact ground.' Ground: 'N123, taxi to the ramp via Charlie, cross Runway 27L.' What should the student read back?
options: 'N123, taxi to the ramp via Charlie, cross Runway two seven left'
'Wilco, N123, taxiing to the ramp via Charlie and crossing 27L'
'Roger, ramp via Charlie, cross two seven left, thank you ground'
'Ramp via Charlie, cross Runway two seven left', since the call sign is only needed on initial contact
steps.why: Read back runway clearances with the complete call sign and runway designator; avoid Roger or Wilco [[7:8|AC 91-73B 7f(4)]] [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18a9]].

steps.s: At the 27L hold line, cleared to cross.
options: Cross slowly with the lights on so tower can watch the airplane the whole way across
Cross immediately on the clearance with eyes on the airport diagram, since tower has the traffic
Wait for the runway entrance lights to turn green before crossing, as the clearance alone is not enough
Scan the full length of 27L and its final, all exterior lights on, then cross without delay
steps.why: Scan the full length and final even when cleared [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(4)]] [[1:368|PHAK 14-34]], all lights on for a crossing [[7:10|AC 91-73B 7h(2)(c)]], and cross in a timely manner [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(6)]].

steps.s: Crossing 27L toward the ramp, the frequency goes silent and ground has said nothing more. Besides the radio, what should the student watch?
options: Nothing else; a silent frequency means no instructions are coming and the clearance stands
The windsock, since a silent tower means the runway in use changed
The tower cab, for light gun signals, since the tower can lose its radio at any time
The ATIS, which will announce any change in her taxi clearance while she crosses
steps.why: The tower may lose communication capability at any time, so monitor guard if able and scan the tower when taxiing or on a runway with a LUAW clearance [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(3)]].

activities.title: Work the numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: A standard Case 1 enhanced taxiway centerline has 12 sets of 9-foot dashes, each followed by a 3-foot gap, and ends with a 6-foot set of dashes. How long is it in feet?
The PHAK says about three runway incursions happen each day at towered airports in the United States. At that rate, about how many happen in a 365-day year?
items.why: 3 x 365 = 1,095 runway incursions a year [[1:365|PHAK 14-31]]. This is arithmetic applied to the PHAK rate.

items.q: You were told to line up and wait with no reason given. You have now been holding 75 seconds without a call. How many more seconds before AC 91-73B says you should call ATC?
items.why: Expect a call within 90 seconds; 90 - 75 = 15 seconds [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(9)]].

items.q: Application: inbound pilots should monitor and talk on the CTAF from 10 miles. At a groundspeed of 90 knots, about how many minutes is that before landing?
items.why: 10 NM / 90 kt x 60 = 6.67 minutes [[33:207|AIM 4-1-9c]]. This is arithmetic applied to the AIM distance.
